content.title: Choosing an Effective Conclusion
content.overview: An effective conclusion synthesizes the main ideas of a paragraph or passage, providing a sense of resolution without introducing new, unrelated topics. On the ACT, you must identify the sentence that best echoes the paragraph's focus and tone while logically closing the discussion.
learning_objectives: Identify the main idea and tone of a paragraph to determine its concluding needs.
Distinguish between sentences that synthesize existing information and those that introduce irrelevant new topics.
Apply the 'Last-Sentence Fit' strategy to select a conclusion that provides logical closure.

sections.title: The Role of a Concluding Sentence
sections.content: A concluding sentence serves as the final 'logical move' of a paragraph. Its primary purpose is to reinforce the central point or summarize the evidence presented. Unlike introductory sentences, which set the stage, or body sentences, which provide evidence, the conclusion should leave the reader with a clear understanding of the paragraph's significance. It must maintain the established tone—whether formal, persuasive, or descriptive—and avoid leaving 'unanswered threads' that would require further explanation.

sections.title: The 'Last-Sentence Fit' Strategy
sections.content: When the ACT asks you to choose the best concluding sentence, follow these three steps: 1. Identify the Main Idea: Briefly summarize what the paragraph is about. 2. Evaluate for Synthesis: Look for a choice that restates this idea in fresh words or draws a logical consequence from the evidence. 3. Eliminate New Topics: Discard any option that introduces a specific detail, requirement, or subject not previously discussed in the paragraph.

sections.title: Recognizing Irrelevant Shifts
sections.content: A common trap on the ACT is the 'Prescriptive Shift.' This occurs when a paragraph describes a situation (e.g., the benefits of solar energy), but the concluding sentence suddenly gives a command or introduces a specific logistical requirement (e.g., 'Therefore, homeowners must check their local zoning laws'). While related to the general subject, these details shift the focus away from the paragraph's core message and are considered incorrect conclusions.

worked_examples.question:
Context: Scientists observed that urban trees reduce local temperatures by providing shade and transpiring water. Tree planting programs increased canopy cover in neighborhoods with highest heat exposure. 

Which choice provides the most effective conclusion to the paragraph?
A. NO CHANGE (The city should measure soil pH before planting trees in any neighborhood.)
B. Planting trees can lower summer temperatures where people need relief most.
C. Trees look nice but require long-term maintenance budgets that cities may not afford.
D. Therefore, officials must choose the tallest tree species available to maximize shade.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the main idea. The paragraph focuses on how trees reduce heat and how programs are targeting hot areas. Step 2: Evaluate Choice A. It introduces 'soil pH,' a new technical detail not mentioned before. Step 3: Evaluate Choice B. It restates the cooling benefit and the targeting of high-heat areas ('where people need relief most'). This synthesizes the paragraph perfectly. Step 4: Evaluate Choice C. It introduces 'maintenance budgets,' a new financial topic. Step 5: Evaluate Choice D. It introduces 'tree species,' a new logistical detail. Choice B is the correct answer.

common_mistakes: Choosing a sentence that is factually true but introduces a new topic not discussed in the paragraph.
Selecting a sentence that is too broad or too narrow for the specific evidence provided.
Picking a 'call to action' (e.g., 'We must do X') when the paragraph was purely descriptive.
Ignoring the tone of the paragraph (e.g., using a very informal conclusion for a scientific passage).
exam_tips: If a choice introduces a specific noun or concept not mentioned in the previous three sentences, it is likely a distractor.
The correct conclusion often acts as a 'mirror' to the topic sentence, restating the main point in a new way.
Read the paragraph with the new sentence included; if it feels like the start of a new paragraph, it is the wrong choice.
content.recap: An effective conclusion reinforces the paragraph's main idea, maintains a consistent tone, and avoids introducing new information. Use the 'Last-Sentence Fit' strategy to ensure the final sentence provides logical closure and synthesis.

knowledge_claims.content: A concluding sentence should synthesize or close the paragraph's main idea rather than starting a new topic.
To choose a conclusion, first identify the paragraph's main idea and then find the choice that restates or extends that idea logically.
It is a mistake to select a concluding sentence that introduces a new, specific detail or logistical requirement not previously mentioned.
An effective conclusion must maintain the same tone (e.g., formal, scientific, or narrative) established in the rest of the paragraph.
A final check for a conclusion is to ensure it leaves no 'unanswered threads' or new questions for the reader.
The 'Prescriptive Shift' is a common distractor where the conclusion suddenly gives a command or advice unrelated to the paragraph's descriptive focus.
A conclusion that 'echoes' the main idea uses fresh words to reinforce the central point made in the topic sentence.
If a paragraph discusses the benefits of a program, the conclusion should reinforce those benefits rather than discussing the program's budget or technical setup.
Unlike a transition sentence, a concluding sentence focuses on resolution within the current paragraph rather than leading into the next one.
A concluding sentence is effective if it follows logically from the preceding evidence provided in the paragraph.
Identify a conclusion as 'too narrow' if it focuses on only one minor detail of the paragraph instead of the overall message.
When testing a choice, read the entire paragraph with the new sentence to see if the flow feels resolved or interrupted.

items.stem:
ENGLISH PASSAGE 1: The Clock Above Alder Street
[1] After three months of fundraising [[a neighborhood restoration crew began]] to repair the brass clock above Alder Street Market. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a market hall built in 1911, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using a laser scan and a box of hand-labeled gears, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] wear marks showed that an earlier repairer had reversed two nearly identical wheels. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because replacement parts would have erased those clues. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the crew cleaned and reused the original wheels. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the clock kept accurate time through a week of rain. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the repair preserved evidence of how local mechanics once solved problems.]]

Which choice best fulfills the goal stated in [10]?

options.F: Everyone was pleased, and the project was finished.
options.G: The result mattered not only because the project worked but also because the repair preserved evidence of how local mechanics once solved problems.
options.H: Many projects use tools, schedules, and careful people.
options.J: There will probably be another project someday.

items.explanation: The correct conclusion links the immediate successful outcome to the broader value established by the passage.

ENGLISH PASSAGE 2: Counting After Dark
[1] After several cloudy evenings [[a coastal ecology class began]] to count juvenile crabs in tide pools after sunset. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a protected inlet beside the school, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using red lamps, quadrats, and waterproof tally sheets, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] the smallest crabs appeared most often under flat stones near eelgrass. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because bright white light changed the animals’ movement. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the class switched to dim red lamps and repeated the first survey. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the second set of counts was more consistent. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the revised method gave park staff a dependable baseline for future surveys.]]

Which choice best fulfills the goal stated in [10]?

options.F: Everyone was pleased, and the project was finished.
options.G: Many projects use tools, schedules, and careful people.
options.H: There will probably be another project someday.
options.J: The result mattered not only because the project worked but also because the revised method gave park staff a dependable baseline for future surveys.

items.explanation: The correct conclusion links the immediate successful outcome to the broader value established by the passage.

videoLesson.title: Craft a Focused Concluding Sentence
videoLesson.description: Recognize how the last sentence echoes the paragraph’s main idea and tone. Restate the core idea in fresh words and end with a logical writing move.
